Part A 1
Hello, Mr. Jaky. It is nice to meet you. Hello, yes, it's great to meet you as well. So, tell me, Mr. Jaky, you are here because an investigation showed microscopic hematuria? Yes, I was in the process of applying for a new job about, I think, six months ago, and I had to get a checkup for insurance purposes. That was when blood was found in the urine sample. Okay, and also you followed up with your GP, is that correct? Yes, that is correct. Since that initial analysis, my GP has run two additional tests that confirm what was previously found. But you have not noticed any blood in your urine or any other urinary problems, right? Yes, right. That is why I was quite shocked when I got the results from that insurance medical. I mean, I consider myself a generally healthy person. I mean, if you were to ask me, I'd say I was doing pretty good health-wise. No major medical issues or anything like that. What about your relatives? Anyone had any problems with their kidneys? You know, renal disease? Not that I'm aware of. So, I have the results of some recent blood investigations that your GP recently had done. Most of the items are within normal ranges, such as your hemoglobin and platelets. Also, your glucose level looks good. I feel a bit nervous coming here, actually. Was there anything out of the normal range? A few things, actually. We took your blood pressure at the beginning of the visit, and it is quite high at 146 over 102. After your investigations, the level of urea was quite high, and also creatinine was out of the normal range. Also, your level of gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase is very high. What is that last thing? I have no idea what it refers to. Well, a high gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase level is compatible with liver disease related to a high alcohol intake. The recommended upper limit of alcohol consumption for men is 28 units per week. I see. Well, I'm going to have to work on that. I often drink a few more units than that per week. Yes, I would definitely recommend that. In fact, I think you need to completely abstain from alcohol for the time being. So does my drinking have anything to do with what's wrong with me, or is something else going on? Well, myscopic hematuria has many renal and urological causes, such as prostatic disease or stones, but the renal impairment, which is indicated by the high urea and creatinine levels, along with the hypertension, point to some form of chronic glomerulonephritis, which is an inflammation of the tiny filters of your kidneys. You can think about it like this. The tiny filters of your kidneys work to remove excess fluid, electrolytes, and waste from your bloodstream and pass them into your urine. How concerned should I be? I mean, is this serious or long-term? Well, about 20% of patients with this condition will go on to develop end-stage renal failure within 20 years of first developing it. So it is something that may affect you in the long run. Also, this condition, along with your declining liver function, is very concerning. We will need, I think, a liver ultrasound and probably also a biopsy to see the extent of the damage to your liver. I see, so no more, this is an...

Part A  2
Hello, Sheila. I have the results of the electrocardiogram and chest X-ray that your GP sent you here to get, but first I just want to review your symptoms to get a complete picture. Okay, sounds fine. So you are a student, is that right? Yes, in my last year of university. And so when did the shortness of breath start? About 10 days ago, I think. At first it was after I rushed from one class to another or had to go upstairs. I mean, I figured it was because I had not been exercising regularly lately. After a couple of days, I couldn't even walk 50 yards without feeling out of breath. And any recent illnesses, like the flu or a bad cold? Yes, about two to three days before I started feeling out of breath, I had a flu-like illness, you know, with the normal generalized muscle aches and fever. I rested for a day or two and then felt better until I started my routine, and that is when the breathlessness got worse, not better. It's hard for me to wrap my head around it. I mean, I'm still young, but I feel like sometimes I'm gasping for breath like a 90-year-old running a marathon. I bet you are also feeling quite tired. Yes, how did you know? I feel extremely tired at times. And also, I have noticed heart palpitations and some discomfort in my chest along with breathlessness. I'm not sure if that is related to the breathlessness, but... Hmm, any changes in routine or lifestyle? I mean, you said you thought the breathlessness might be due to lack of exercise. I mean, it has been a tough semester at uni, so I have not been exercising as much as I would like, but I still managed to go for a run two or three times a week. Oh, okay, so you would say you are generally a fit person? And any experimentation with drugs? No, no substance abuse. I mean, I know what you're thinking, young person in uni, must want to experiment, but no, that's not me. So what does all this mean? I mean, you've heard my symptoms now and you have my test. So your chest x-ray was normal, which is good, but I'm afraid there are some abnormalities in your ECG. This, along with the symptoms you described of fatigue, shortness of breath, pericardial pain, and palpitations, points to myocarditis. The flu-like illness you described is also compatible with this disease. I asked about substance abuse because one cause of myocarditis is cocaine use. So... I see, I get it. You have to ask. Okay, so what does that mean exactly? Viral myocarditis, is it something wrong with my lungs or my heart or... Myocarditis is an inflammation of the heart muscle, and the viral part refers to the fact that a virus is the cause. There are a number of viruses that can cause this problem, including coxsackie B and A, echovirus, and varicella. Isn't varicella chickenpox? Yes, it is. So is this serious? Well, first we'll need to perform an echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis, and we'll also do some investigations to test for the cause of the myocarditis. Based on the fact that your chest x-ray was normal, the myocarditis is likely mild. So that is the good news. The maybe not so great news is that you will need to be on bed rest for a while. Most cases of myocarditis are benign and cardiac function returns to normal, but resting is an important part of treatment. That will be a bit difficult, but I will have to see what arrangements I can make at uni to lighten my load for the next.
